newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD-Australia markets eyeing imports.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD-Australia markets eyeing imports.

text.p: As Australian markets wind down ahead of the Christmas/New Year period, emphasis will be on the U.S. data and local import and export figures.

Wednesday's release of November imports data will be the lone key domestic figure for the week, and for the remainder of 1996. Imports are expected to be boosted by the possible inclusion of aircrat, valued at about A$100 million, and as a result may record their fourth consecutive rise.

Economists' expectations for imports, which to date are up 7.0 percent despite weakness in the economy, are in a range of a fall of 2.3 percent to a rise of five percent. The appreciaton of the Australian dollar, which cuts into the value of imports in local currency terms, should weigh on the figure, however.

Talk over whether the Reserve Bank will chop rates again soon following last week's 0.5 percentage points cut continues to circulate in the markets but economists have ruled out another cut soon as inflation has little room to fall further.
Reserve Bank Deputy Governor Graham Thompson speaks in Sydney on Tuesday.
Although it is the first appearance by a senior RBA official since last Wednesday's rate cut, Thompson's speech to a superannuation conference is not expected to generate too much for the market.
Other Australian data due for release include the October Westpac leading index and DEETYA December skilled vacancies, both on Wednesday.
But while there are few Australian statistics being released, there could be plenty of market action based on U.S. developments, with investors apparently jumping at every sign of inflation.
Monday's release of U.S. industrial production figures for November are expected to record an increase.
More importantly, anticipation is likely to mount ahead of the outcome of Tuesday's December Federal Open market Committee (FOMC) meeting.
If the Fed signals a bias toward tightening, then bond yields could rise while the share market falls.
No change in U.S. rates is expected to follow the meeting.

But given Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's recent comments thath the U.S. inflation outlook remains uncertain, it's unlikely the FOMC meeting will help settle what has become a very jittery market, analysts said.
Other U.S. data out this week include housing starts on Tuesday, and third-quarter GDP (final) on Friday.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS (Fri 10-yr cash 7.43 pct, 3-yr cash 6.45)

Australian bonds will the start the week on solid footing, after U.S. Treasuries closed higher. The 6-1/2 percent 30-year benchmark U.S. Treasury bond ended up 20/32 at 99-00. Its yield slipped to 6.58 percent against 6.62 in the previous session.

The Australian market found a tentative base on Friday after a volatile trading week which saw the surprise cut in official rates overshadowed by jittery trading in both U.S. Treasury and equity markets. While such conditions could continue this week, traders expect turnover to slow as investors start to close their books for 1996. However, Monday's trade could be artifically active with the closing out of the December bond futures contracts.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri close US$0.7928/33, NY $0.7915/20)

The Australian dollar starts the week steady after dipping in New York on Friday. Interim support was seen at US$0.7910 and US$0.7890 on Friday, with the key level being US$0.7850. The currency needs to clear US$0.7950 to counter the risk of a deeper correction and would have to break US$0.8050 to revive the uptrend interrupted by the Australian interest rate cut.
Barring a major development from Tuesday's U.S. FOMC meeting, scheduled economic data is unlikely to hold much sway on the value of the Australian dollar.

However, economists noted that the spot rate is now below its nine and 30-day moving averages and that momentum has turned. Longer term, the local unit should begin to rise by mid-1997 as stronger world growth lifts commodity prices, Syntec Economic Services said in a report.
AUSTRALIAN SHARES (Friday All Ords 2316.5, down 23.1)
The Australian share market may be in for a rough ride at the start of the week in response to Friday's mostly weaker closing in U.S. stocks.
The Australian share market ended on Friday with its third consecutive fall in response to the overnight plunge on Wall Street, although investors did regain some confidence in the afternoon session.
The Dow Industrials ended Friday up one at about 6304, but was left 77 points lower on the week.

"If the Dow can stabilise and more particularly if bond rates can stabilise then the market will go up quite strongly next week," said Greg Matthews, executive director of Australian equities at fund manager Mercantile Mutual.
"But if the U.S. market falls then our market will fall in the short term as well," he said.
